documents.title: ICCS practical guidelines clinical flow cytometry

chunks.content: 1 Introduction The diagnosis of Paroxysmal Nocturnal Hemoglobinuria (PNH) relies on detecting the loss of the glycosyl‐phosphatidyl inositol (GPI)‐anchored surface molecules from both white blood cells (WBCs) and red blood cells (RBCs) by flow cytometry [ , , ], despite the underlying molecular mechanism involving somatic mutations of the X‐linked phosphatidyl‐inositol glycan Class A ( PIGA ) gene [ , ]. Significant progress has been made since the use of the FLAER reagent [ , ] and the publication of international recommendations [ , , , , ]. Various sizes of the PNH clone, consisting of totally deficient cells (type III) alone or associated with partially deficient cells (type II) [ ], can be quantified by flow cytometry. The International PNH Interest Group (IPIG) has classified disease with PNH clones into three subtypes: classical PNH, which includes hemolytic and thrombotic patients who have evidence of PNH clones in the absence of another bone marrow failure disorder; PNH in the context of other primary bone marrow disorders, such as aplastic anemia and myelodysplastic neoplasms; and subclinical PNH, in which patients have small PNH clones but no clinical or laboratory evidence of hemolysis or thrombosis [ ]. Patients with classical PNH typically have higher clone sizes in WBCs; monocyte and neutrophil clone sizes classically correlate well at the time of diagnosis than patients in other categories; these patients also, by definition, have evidence of hemolysis in the form of elevated LDH and reticulocyte counts. RBC clone sizes, however, are less reliable as these are typically lower in untreated patients with PNH due to hemolysis and/or transfusion. Importantly, the size of the neutrophil clone is relevant to the thrombosis risk for the classical PNH patient [ ]. Patients with subclinical PNH have the smallest clone sizes of any of the IPIG classification groups [ , , , , , ]. Early diagnosis of PNH is essential for providing optimal care and treatment if clinically indicated [ , , , , ]. Since flow cytometry is the gold standard to detect PNH clones, performing the assay on fresh cells is crucial to ensure high‐quality results. Therefore, the French PNH working group, initiated in 2010 after the publication of the first international recommendations [ ], aimed to harmonize diagnostic practices throughout the country. First, a dedicated workshop was conducted to evaluate different flow cytometry methods in a multiplatform and multicenter approach. Then, we developed in 2013 a quality control scheme for the French‐speaking region based on the international recommendations for PNH screening [ ]. This interlaboratory comparison program is still ongoing, and we report here on our group's 10‐year experience, during which we successfully built a strong network of cytometrists. 2 2010—The Start With a Dedicated Workshop for <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">PNH</styled-content> Testing on <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">WBCs</styled-content> In 2010, the first publication of the international recommendations highlighted the relevance of a new reagent for flow cytometry called FLAER, an inactivated bacterial toxin able to bind to all GPI‐anchored proteins on leucocytes and to detect their deficiency [ , , ]. In order to share these guidelines, the French PNH working group was established in 2010. Inspired by the General de Gaulle's famous “18th of June Call,” we initiated a dedicated workshop following our call on June 18, 2010, marking the first French‐speaking meeting focused on PNH diagnosis and high‐sensitivity assays in WBCs. Thirty‐five French and Belgian laboratories participated in this multicenter study aimed at evaluating various flow cytometry methods for PNH testing on WBCs across multiple platforms. 2.1 Succeeding in Multicenter Instrument Harmonization The 35 centers were equipped with multiparameter flow cytometers including 8‐color/3‐laser FACSCanto II (BD Biosciences, San Jose CA, USA) in 14 laboratories, 5‐color/1‐laser FC500 (Beckman‐Coulter, Miami FL, USA) in 13 laboratories, and 10‐color/3‐laser Navios (Beckman‐Coulter) in 8 laboratories. The harmonization of the instrument settings was achieved in the 18 centers outfitted with 3‐laser flow cytometers using 8‐peak Rainbow bead calibration particles, after conversion of the fluorescent intensity target values [ ] (Figure ). As an illustration, the coefficients of variation (CVs) were below 5% for FITC, PE, PerCP‐Cy5.5/PC5.5, APC, and V450/PB fluorescence channels, yet slightly increased for the PE‐Cy7 channel to 5.7%, as expected [ ]. 2.2 Achieving a 10<sup>−4</sup> Limit of Detection in a Harmonized Multicenter Approach In order to investigate the technical limit of PNH testing in a multicenter approach, the participating centers were asked to perform three different staining procedures on WBCs, after implementing the harmonization described above. Two‐color (CD11b/CD55‐CD59 [ ]) and 6‐color combinations, including or not the FLAER reagent (FLAER/CD24/CD14/CD33/CD15/CD45 or CD55/CD24/CD14/CD33/CD15/CD45 in one or two tubes depending on the cytometer type) were proposed. At that time, neither panel option included CD64 for monocyte gating. The gating strategy used was the one recommended by the international guidelines [ ]. in a Harmonized Multicenter Approach In order to investigate the technical limit of PNH testing in a multicenter approach, the participating centers were asked to perform three different staining procedures on WBCs, after implementing the harmonization described above. Two‐color (CD11b/CD55‐CD59 [ ]) and 6‐color combinations, including or not the FLAER reagent (FLAER/CD24/CD14/CD33/CD15/CD45 or CD55/CD24/CD14/CD33/CD15/CD45 in one or two tubes depending on the cytometer type) were proposed. At that time, neither panel option included CD64 for monocyte gating. The gating strategy used was the one recommended by the international guidelines [ ]. The purpose of that workshop was to develop a high‐sensitivity test dedicated to WBCs in a harmonized multicenter approach. In this study, the minimal requirements for defining a PNH population were the observation of at least 20 events with total absence of GPI‐linked protein expression (type III cells). Hence, all participants were asked to acquire a minimum of 200,000 neutrophils in order to reach the optimal limit of detection. Three hundred and five peripheral blood samples were obtained from 75 locally diagnosed PNH patients (PNH clones ranging from 0.08% to 99.95%), 62 patients with circulating immature granulocytes, and 41 patients with MDS, as well as 127 controls. The initial results gathered from in‐house gating strategies highlighted the need for harmonized procedures and participant education, which were subsequently implemented. A higher cellular background was observed in MDS samples and in those with immature granulocytes. By employing harmonized multiparametric approaches with both 6‐color combinations and harmonized gating strategies procedures across multiplatforms, we achieved a 10 −4 limit of detection [ ]. For robust quantification of minor PNH clones, the use of the FLAER is recommended [ ]. This reagent was included in all the files generated for our interlaboratory comparison program (see below). 3 2013–2024—Highlights From the 10‐Year Experience of <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">PNH</styled-content> Interlaboratory Comparison Program The insights gained from the workshop highlighted that, for PNH diagnosis by flow cytometry, both technical proficiency and the accuracy of interpretation and reporting are equally critical. UK NEQAS for Leucocyte Immunophenotyping proposes stabilized samples for PNH in their External Quality Assessment (EQA) programs [ , ]. However, there was a need for a French‐speaking program, particularly for the report drafting. Therefore, we have developed since 2013 a quality control scheme for the French‐speaking region, aligned with the first international guidelines for PNH screening [ ]. This program aims to improve PNH diagnosis practices by analyzing the three recommended different populations in peripheral blood: neutrophils, monocytes, and RBCs. 3.1 Proposing a Two‐Step Survey Program We propose a 1‐year, two‐step survey program to any volunteering clinical laboratories from French‐speaking countries [ ]. It consists of running two successive surveys: a virtual survey based on raw data file analysis to harmonize data interpretation and quality of reports, and a second survey based on a fresh whole‐blood sample analysis to examine the whole process, from the technical procedure to the final report, and appreciate the employed methods in the participating laboratories. Regarding virtual cases, raw data files sent to the centers are currently generated simultaneously by different cytometers: BD Biosciences instruments (BD FACSCanto II and FACSLyric, this latter being used since 2021) and Beckman Coulter instruments (Navios and DxFLEX, this latter being used since 2023). In the context of the fresh survey, whole blood samples are provided by Dr. Bernard Drenou (Groupe Hospitalier de la Région Mulhouse Sud Alsace) in accordance with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki, and participants are asked to use their own routine flow cytometric procedures immediately after reception. Following the international guidelines [ ], participants are instructed to report the PNH clone size as follows: only the total PNH clone size in both the WBCs (neutrophils and monocytes) should be included in the conclusion, alongside the percentage of type II and type III RBCs and the total RBC clone size. In France, data on type II and type III percentages in WBCs are also collected, along with type II and type III percentages in RBCs, due to the establishment of the National Observatory of PNH clones. It is important to note that in cases where there is no clear distinction between PNH type II and type III RBCs, it is recommended to report a combined population of RBCs with CD59 deficiency, accompanied by a comment explaining the reason, rather than setting arbitrary regions for type II and type III [ ]. For the statistical analysis of the participant results, a robust statistical method is used in compliance with the ISO/International Electrotechnical Commission 17043 [ ] requirement concerning the proficiency of the interlaboratory quality controllers. Robust mean, coefficient of variation (CV), standard deviation (SD), and z score are calculated for type II, type III, and total PNH cell subsets across the three analyzed lineages (neutrophils, monocytes, and RBCs). For the statistical analysis of the participant results, a robust statistical method is used in compliance with the ISO/International Electrotechnical Commission 17043 [ ] requirement concerning the proficiency of the interlaboratory quality controllers. Robust mean, coefficient of variation (CV), standard deviation (SD), and z score are calculated for type II, type III, and total PNH cell subsets across the three analyzed lineages (neutrophils, monocytes, and RBCs). These metrics are provided to each participant in a private report for both virtual and fresh cases with a PNH clone. In case where no PNH clone is detected, only the robust mean, CV, and SD of the number of analyzed cells are provided, along with the assay sensitivity for the three different lineages included. All private reports incorporate a standard interpretation of the results developed by the group of experts. Eventually, the participants also receive a general report on each of the two different surveys [ ]. 3.2 Demonstrating the Strong Commitment From French‐Speaking Laboratories Throughout the 10‐Year Program The first 2013 edition of the interlaboratory comparison program succeeded in rallying 49 participants from voluntary centers [ ]. Over the last 10 years, the number of participants slightly increased (Figure ), achieving nearly 60 participants in 2023, including the four expert centers: 50 French metropolitan, one French overseas, four Belgian, one Swiss, and one Moroccan (Figure ). This demonstrates a strong commitment from the registered centers throughout the program duration. We believe that this participant engagement relies on both the quality of the flow cytometry files provided and the diverse PNH clinical situations that illustrate “real‐life” issues. Over the past 10 years, nine fresh cases (FC) were provided to the participants (Figure ), featuring various clone sizes across the three lineages, ranging from 0.15% to 98.8% on neutrophils. We collected the mean and the coefficient of variation for each survey (Table ). Regardless of the lineage, smaller clone sizes are associated with a wider coefficient of variation. Notably, the percentage of type II RBCs, ranging from 0.03% to 7.42%, is often associated with a very large coefficient of variation, highlighting the challenges in delineating this cell type, as it has been elegantly recently demonstrated [ ]. 3.3 Offering Insights Into Various <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">PNH</styled-content> Clinical Situations The interlaboratory comparison program has evolved over the last 10 years, particularly to align with the revised international guidelines [ , , , ]. New panels for WBC analysis of virtual cases were proposed, notably for monocyte gating. CD64 has been defined as the recommended non‐GPI linked marker for monocyte identification instead of CD33. Therefore, we chose to modify in 2019 the staining of the samples used for the virtual cases and have since proposed panels that include either CD64 or CD33. However, we decided not to implement CD157, despite its potential to replace both CD24 and CD14 [ ], since several CD157‐negative, non‐PNH cases have been reported [ ]. Besides, owing to the strong emphasis placed on the RBC analysis in the revised recommendations, we proposed cases focusing on the importance of studying that lineage. Indeed, we proposed a virtual case involving a 70‐year‐old woman with aplastic anemia. The assay sensitivity on monocytes did not allow for a conclusion, while GPI‐deficient cells were detected in neutrophils and estimated at 0.15%. In this case, analysis on RBCs proved invaluable, as it confirmed the presence of a PNH clone with a size of 0.04% ( the figures indicated were obtained using the FACSCanto II cytometer, see Figure , upper panels). Another virtual case highlighted the interest of the PNH clone size quantification on RBCs. It involved a 30‐year‐old man diagnosed with classical PNH, presenting a major PNH clone at 93.12% on neutrophils and 94.2% on monocytes, and 33.00% on RBCs at diagnosis. The files sent to the participants corresponded to the 1‐year follow‐up during eculizumab treatment [ ]. The clone size slightly increased on WBCs (96.99% on neutrophils and 95.9% on monocytes; the figures indicated were obtained using the FACSCanto II cytometer, see Figure , upper panels). An expected increase in size to 92.56% was observed in RBCs, indicating successful therapy, as eculizumab prevents hemolysis of the GPI‐deficient PNH RBCs [ ]. Among the 20 surveys, we challenged the participants with the case of a 57‐year‐old woman with aplastic anemia who underwent bone marrow transplantation. The PNH clone, initially estimated at 1.40% on neutrophils, 7.1% on monocytes, and 0.36% on RBCs at diagnosis ( the figures indicated were obtained using the Navios cytometer, see Figure , lower panels), disappeared in the follow‐up sample (Figure ). 3.4 Improving Practices in <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">PNH</styled-content> Diagnosis Since reporting is a crucial part

The PNH clone, initially estimated at 1.40% on neutrophils, 7.1% on monocytes, and 0.36% on RBCs at diagnosis ( the figures indicated were obtained using the Navios cytometer, see Figure , lower panels), disappeared in the follow‐up sample (Figure ). 3.4 Improving Practices in <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">PNH</styled-content> Diagnosis Since reporting is a crucial part of the process, we created a compact guide designed to fit in a laboratory coat pocket, aimed at harmonizing PNH test conclusions in accordance with the successive international recommendations [ , , , , ]. We analyzed the conformity of the final reports provided by the participants in cases of both PNH clone presence (Figure ) and absence (Figure ). Over the past 10 years, we have proudly observed a significant increase in conformity for both clinical situations, reaching 96%. 3.5 Towards the Next Workshop Dedicated to <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">RBC</styled-content> Assay The initial workshop we conducted played a crucial role in the harmonization of PNH testing in France. While we focused on implementing WBC analysis for PNH testing, there is now a pressing need to improve the RBC assay. We are planning to organize a dedicated workshop in 2025 to present the newly developed screening test involving immature RBCs (iRBCs) [ ]. Indeed, the PNH clone size evaluated in CD71+ RBCs appears to be larger than in mature RBCs and correlates with that in both neutrophils and monocytes [ ]. The major advantage of the CD71 addition is the more reliable separation between true PNH type II and PNH type III cells versus the incorrect inclusion of transfused cells into the PNH RBC clone. The reason for the almost identical PNH clone size between the lineages is that the iRBCs are not prone to complement‐mediated lysis. Moreover, detection of C3d deposit on RBCs by flow cytometry in anti‐C5‐treated patients may be of interest for assessing extravascular hemolysis [ ]. 4 A Strong Network of Cytometrists Built in France Following the diagnostic practice harmonization spread in France since 2013 through our ongoing inter‐laboratory comparison program, our PNH working group initiated a nationwide multicenter prospective observational study on February 29, 2016, in order to collect all PNH cases or GPI‐deficient cells above 0.01%. The first main objective is to monitor the long‐term evolution of minor PNH clones < 1%, which represent over one third of positive samples [ ], using high‐resolution flow cytometry, as previous evaluations showed the disappearance of PNH clones in 6%–24% of patients with bone marrow failure over 3–5 years with a 2‐color flow cytometry procedure [ , ]. The second objective aims to further investigate the relevance of classifying type II and type III PNH cells in WBCs in clones larger than 1%, as the significance of this distinction—unlike in RBCs—remains unclear. The collected data at diagnosis and during long‐term follow‐up are currently under analysis. This experience and the strong network of cytometrists we have built since the workshop conducted in 2010 led us to create in 2018 the French‐speaking flow cytometry association in Hematology, namely the CytHem for Cytometry in Hematology ( https://www.cythem.fr ). Its main purpose is to harmonize the diagnostic practices by sharing technical protocols and gating strategies for the different instruments equipping the routine laboratories. Eleven working groups have been created, each dedicated to a specific hemopathy or disease group (PNH, chronic myelomonocytic leukemia, myelodysplastic neoplasms, acute myeloid leukemia, mature B‐cell neoplasms, central nervous lymphomas, granular lymphocytic leukemia, lymphoblastic leukemia, Sezary Syndrome, plasma cell neoplasms), except CytHem‐questions, which was established to address practical issues, provide information, and manage In Vitro Diagnosis Regulations (IVDR) concerns. Each disease working group is closely related to a French‐speaking clinical association. The PNH working group is indeed working alongside the rare immuno‐hematological diseases (MaRIH) healthcare network ( https://marih.fr ).
